analysis.title: US Equities Weekly Rundown: Positioning, Flows, and Observations Across the Floor
key_insights: The S&P 500 fell 1.9% on the week and the Nasdaq 100 fell 5.5%, its worst week since April 2025. The desk attributes the move to stress in credit markets and the AI trade, higher than expected inflation prints, and a resilient US economy.

Prime book US long/short net leverage fell 3.2 points to 43.7%, the largest weekly decline since the week of Liberation Day in April 2025 and the 0th percentile over five years. Gross leverage rose 0.9 points to 213.9%. The fundamental long/short ratio fell 3.3% to 1.513, also the 0th percentile over five years.

US equities were net sold on the week (-0.9 SDs over one year), led by long and short sales in single stocks, the largest net selling in 8 weeks. 8 of 11 sectors were net sold. Health Care, Communication Services and Staples were net bought, which the desk reads as an incrementally defensive posture.

Info Tech was the worst performing and most net sold sector (-1.6 SDs), with long sales outpacing short sales 6 to 1. Semis made up 57% of the dollar net selling within Info Tech. Semis now make up 9.5% of total US net market value on the Prime book.

Semis fell eight consecutive sessions, the longest streak since May 2006, with memory (MU and SNDK) down in 7 of 8 sessions. Claims of a breakthrough in memory from China's CXMT were the proximate catalyst. The desk reads the move more as a broad global cooling of the AI bottleneck trade, with Korea the clearest expression (KOSPI -14% on the week).

AI credit stress is bleeding into equities. CDS and high-yield spreads widened sharply in the second half of the week, and the desk cites concern about the capacity to finance parts of the AI ecosystem. Neocloud stocks fell 24.82% on the week (GSXUNEOC), optical networks 21.42% and memory 16.57%.

The desk's global AI basket (GSXGGLAI) saw its second-largest net selling in a year on Wednesday. Selling over Oct 8-15 was roughly on par with the late-July episode and the largest since March 2022. The desk says the AI trade is still long, at roughly 6/10 on length, and materially cleaner than June and July. Its sentiment indicator has been negative for six straight weeks.

The desk distinguishes this selloff from July's, which it called largely technical. This one has opened a debate over which concern is most acute into year-end: earnings, elections, rates and credit, return on invested capital, or inflation.

Macro: a hot CPI print on Wednesday raised fears of an October Fed hike. A neutral stance from Warsh on Thursday night eased them, with markets pricing about a 17% chance of a hike before the Fed blackout and 85% by December. GS economists still expect the next hike in December. Brent rallied above $110 a barrel for the first time since late May on stalled US/Iran talks.

Under the index surface, breadth recovered, with an average of 343 S&P names up on the week. Late-week leadership broadened to RTY > SPX > NDX. Quality was strong (GSP1QUAL +4.20%) and Mag7 held up through Thursday on a flight-to-safety bid. Banks were mixed after earnings and likely served as a funding short for AI weakness.

Asset managers and hedge funds were both better for sale on the week. Both sold tech and macro products. Asset managers saw demand in financials and consumer discretionary, and hedge funds saw small demand in communication services.

Hedge funds net sold US Financials for the first time in 5 weeks (-1.2 SDs) as large banks began reporting, with short sales outpacing long buys 4.4 to 1. Capital markets, insurance and payment processors were the most net sold subsectors, while consumer finance and banks were modestly net bought.

Health Care was the best performing and most net bought sector (+1.7 SDs), driven by short covers. The desk reads this as a continued risk unwind because the sector's gross trading activity fell for a fifth straight week. Biotech saw the largest de-grossing in the sector, and the US Biotech long/short ratio is 3.12.

CTAs (trend followers) are expected to buy some government bond futures in the baseline scenario. The desk estimates they are short $164mm/bp of DV01 globally and covered $12mm/bp last week. It expects a further $20mm of covering over one week and $64mm over one month, which would leave them still short.

In equities, the desk expects CTAs to be only modestly net long. It forecasts $18bn of buying over one week and $30bn over one month in the baseline, led by European products and more neutral in US markets, after $55bn of global selling over the past month. CTA performance is up nearly 17% on the year.

VIX futures were aggressively bought on Friday afternoon, taking VIX to its highest level since July. QQQ has closed lower five sessions in a row, but the vol market only fully reacted late Friday. VVIX jumped 17 points, one of the largest one-day moves in four years. Front month VIX outperformed its beta to SPX by 1.5 vols, the most since April. Asset managers entered the session with VIX futures positioning at the shortest on record.

Mag7 average 3-month implied volatility was near multi-year lows despite full positioning, and the desk says downside protection is still not prohibitively expensive. It says 3-month puts on its GSX1MEGA basket continue to screen well as a hedge through year-end.

Over $8 billion flowed into levered ETFs in four days, the largest weekly inflow in the desk's dataset, as investors try to find the bottom in AI. SOXL (3x semis) took in about $6 billion this week, tracking its largest weekly and rolling 5-day haul ever. Levered ETF flows have historically been strongest on -2 sigma down days. Levered and inverse ETFs hold $176 billion in assets and $444 billion in gross exposure, and invested units have net increased, so a market recovery could act as a growth catalyst for the complex.

Thematic baskets desk: on Wednesday Oct 14 the S&P 500 had its first 1% decline since July while the S&P 500 ex-AI index (SPXXAI) rose 61bps. The desk likes buying SPXXAI and sees an attractive entry point to rotate into the broader non-AI market. It cites three catalysts: AI datacenter high-yield credit stress, accelerating Chinese hardware exports (about 36% more than a year ago), and a hotter US inflation backdrop that is unfriendly to long-duration, capex-heavy growth stories.

TMT specialists: HF VIP TMT basket is down 13% since 10/8 and the GS TMT momentum pair fell 14% in 3 days. Focus turns to whether positive AI-complex earnings prints will be rewarded in share prices and arrest the negative momentum.

Consumer outperformed (Staples +5%, Discretionary +3%, Retail and Restaurants +4.5%), which the specialist attributes largely to positioning and rotation, since consumer has acted as the short leg of the momentum trade. Better high-frequency data and a September Retail Sales beat helped. Next week's consumer earnings are expected to be mixed, with top-line upside expected at PG and TSCO.

Financials and REITs rose 2-3% as the market broadened out of tech. Winners were defensive names (P&C insurance, exchanges, healthcare REITs), consumer-exposed names (payments, lodging REITs) and information services. Laggards were cyclicals (industrial REITs, banks) and capital markets (alts, investment banks). BLK was a preferred long with solid follow-through.

Healthcare outperformed (XLV +3.3% vs SPY -2% and QQQ -5%) on the AI and momentum slide and broadening rotation. Q3 earnings reactions were mixed (JNJ -5.7%, UNH -20bps after being up 6% pre-market). Unwind themes persisted in small and mid-cap biotech and in AI drug discovery tools and diagnostics (GSHLCTOO -10% from its early-October peak after a 90% move from May).

Week ahead: the S&P implied move through Friday 10/23 is 1.33%. Macro data is light and the Fed is in blackout. About 14% of S&P market cap reports, weighted to energy, industrials and materials, with META and TSLA on Wednesday the biggest names. Financials earnings broaden to AXP, BX, CBRE, MCO, MSCI and regional banks.

Operational note for options traders: from Monday Oct 19, 2026, Cboe Options (C1) and NYSE American Options introduce extended hours of 7:30-9:25 AM ET pre-market and 4:00-4:15 PM ET post-market for 29 tickers. Regular hours run 9:30 AM to 4:00 PM ET, and the listed ETF options (GLD, IWM, QQQ, SPY, XLF) already trade until 4:15 PM ET.
A supportive datapoint into earnings season is the Nasdaq 100 forward P/E back near 21x, the lows since the AI cycle began in 2023.

Levered ETF inflows of over $8 billion in four days, including about $6 billion into SOXL, show dip-buying demand in AI and semis.

geopolitical: US/Iran tensions show little progress, pushing Brent futures above $110 a barrel for the first time since late May.

US mid-term elections are cited among the concerns investors are weighing into year-end.

tension_points.bull_case: Earnings season kicks off next week with focus on AI-complex prints. The Nasdaq 100 forward P/E has fallen to about 21x, the lowest since 2023. Levered ETF dip-buying has increased invested units, and the desk says that if conditions improve this demand could be a growth catalyst.
tension_points.bear_case: AI datacenter high-yield credit is under scrutiny, Chinese hardware exports are up about 36% from a year ago, and core CPI (+33bps) and core PPI (+70bps) came in above consensus. The desk expects index dispersion between SPX and SPXXAI to narrow as AI headline risk catches up with pricing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Positive earnings prints in the AI complex that are not rewarded in share prices, which would leave the negative sentiment and price momentum intact.

tension_points.bull_case: The AI trade is still long but roughly 6/10 on length and materially cleaner than June and July, and downside protection is not prohibitively expensive.
tension_points.bear_case: Unlike July's pullback, which investors called technical, this episode has opened a real debate over which wall of worry is most acute into year-end (earnings, elections, rates and credit, ROIC, inflation).
